### Threshold tuning, and why it is the most delicate part of the notebook

Sattler's split criterion is:

```
split when   ||sum of deltas|| < eps1   AND   max ||individual delta|| > eps2
```

The reasoning: at a stationary point of a *single* data distribution the client updates
cancel, so their sum is near zero (hence `eps1`), while the individual updates are not (hence
`eps2`). **A group whose mean update has gone quiet while its members are still moving hard is
a group being pulled in two directions at once**: the signature of two distributions sharing
one model.

**Why the published constants (0.4, 1.6) are not used.** They assume a converged federation.
Over six rounds ours has not converged, and those values never fire on our data. Sattler
treats `eps1` and `eps2` as **per-experiment quantities**, so tuning them follows the paper
rather than departing from it.

**Why tuning happens on an attacker-free warmup.** This is not a detail, it is the difference
between the claim being meaningful and not. Tuning on a run containing the attacker would
produce a criterion **fitted to the attack it is supposed to be blind to**, and every
downstream number would then describe a server that had already seen what we claim it cannot
see. Four honest rounds, `warm`, no `attack=` argument.

**Why `margin=1.5` and `× 0.5`.** `eps1 = ||sum d|| × 1.5` sits *above* the summed-delta norm
at the end of warmup, so the criterion fires once the mixture has settled. `eps2 = max ||d|| ×
0.5` sits *below* the largest individual norm, so it keeps firing afterwards.

> **This was got wrong twice, in both directions, and both failures were silent.**
>
> **Attempt 1** put `eps1` *above* the summed norm by too much, so the criterion fired
> constantly and shattered the federation into singletons.
>
> **Attempt 2** tuned `eps2` from **round 1** instead of the last warmup round. Both criterion
> quantities decay as the federation trains, and they decay together: on label-permuted MNIST,
> head scope, `max ||d||` falls from 0.9351 at round 1 to 0.3482 by round 8. Tuning from round
> 1 gives `eps2 = 0.5 × 0.94 = 0.47`, but `max ||d||` later falls to 0.348, so the condition
> `max ||d|| > eps2` becomes **permanently unsatisfiable** and the clusterer silently never
> splits. No error, no warning, just a federation that stays whole and an infiltration column
> full of NaN.
>
> This is why `tune_thresholds` **prints what it chose**: the five `[sattler]` lines in the
> output above. A tuning step that fails silently is worse than one that crashes.

### The four correctness guards in this cell

**1. `beta=0` is the control.** The same attacker object, same code path, same seeds, with the
commitment dial at zero. It reduces the mechanism to honest training. Because the control runs
through the attack machinery rather than around it, any effect is attributable to the
imitation rather than to some difference in the pipeline.

**2. `set_global_seeds(s)` is called twice**: once before the warmup and again before the
measured run. Model initialisation is therefore identical between the control and the attacked
condition on a given seed, so the two differ only in the attack.

**3. `clus.reset()`.** `SattlerCosineClusterer` keeps a persistent cluster tree across rounds
because **splits are permanent**: the tree is only ever refined, never re-merged. Reusing an
un-reset clusterer between conditions would carry the control's split into the attacked run.

**4. `recursive=False, max_clusters=2`.** The published algorithm is recursive, splitting until
no group meets the criterion. Here it is limited to one split, so the number of clusters is
fixed and "infiltration" means one thing rather than varying with the round. This is a
**documented deviation**, made for measurability, and it is what IFCA and PACFL do anyway.

### The results

**Placement: 1.000 against a 0.000 control**, zero-width intervals on both. Unanimous.

**Accuracy: 0.843 attacked against 0.833 control**: and the verdict column says **"not
distinguishable from baseline"**, because the intervals ([0.817, 0.868] and [0.806, 0.855])
overlap substantially.

Note the cost prints as `-0.0101`: the attacker's federation ended up *very slightly more*
accurate. That is noise, and the machinery correctly refuses to call it an effect in either
direction.

### Why "imitation is free" is the defence-relevant finding

Resampling changes **which** distribution the model learns, not **how well** it learns one. The
attacker trains on a perfectly coherent dataset, just a different one from its own. There is
no degradation, no instability, no anomaly.

**A defence looking for a degraded or anomalous attacker will not find one, because there is
nothing degraded about it.** That closes off utility-based detection entirely, and it is
recorded in `DEFENSE_NOTES.md` §11.1 as one of the two defence families this study rules out.

# Cells 20 to 21, Part 6: prior-editing as a real attack

## Cell 20, markdown

```markdown
## Part 6. Prior-editing, run as an attack rather than shown on paper

Part 3 derived the bias shift arithmetically. This runs it, because "unbounded" is a claim
about behaviour and has to be measured.

The test is the class the attacker holds **none** of. Resampling left it at zero, because
you cannot draw what you do not have. If prior-editing can make the model claim that class,
the two routes differ in kind rather than only in degree.
```

**Why this part exists at all.** Cell 14 showed the arithmetic. Arithmetic is not evidence
about behaviour: the bias sits behind a softmax, after a BatchNorm-laden trunk, and the claim
that the model's *actual output* moves as the algebra says is a claim that has to be measured.
This part measures it.

**Why the zero-holding class is the right test.** It is the one place the two routes must
differ if they differ at all. Everywhere else resampling already succeeds, so a comparison
there would show nothing.

---

## Cell 21, code, running prior-editing

```python
# Run the prior-edit mechanism, then read the model's ACTUAL output distribution
# off the probe set. The comparison that matters is the class with zero holdings.
prior_rows = []
for s in CONFIG["SEEDS"]:
    b_pr = bundle(s)
    H_pr = partition_label_hists(b_pr)
    home_pr, tgt_pr, tgt_mem_pr = sides(b_pr)
    profile_pr = group_profile(b_pr, tgt_pr)
    own_pr = H_pr[CONFIG["ATTACKER"]]

    atk = ClusterSteering(malicious_clients=[CONFIG["ATTACKER"]],
                          target_members=tgt_mem_pr, mechanism="prior", beta=1.0,
                          num_classes=b_pr.num_classes, arch=CONFIG["ARCH"],
                          input_shape=b_pr.input_shape, seed=s)
    atk.target_hist = profile_pr
    atk.own_data = {CONFIG["ATTACKER"]: b_pr.client_data[CONFIG["ATTACKER"]]}

    set_global_seeds(s, backend="torch")
    srv_pr = TorchFederatedServer(b_pr.input_shape, b_pr.num_classes,
                                  SattlerCosineClusterer(eps1=-1.0, scope="head"),
                                  arch=CONFIG["ARCH"], attack=atk,
                                  n_clusters=CONFIG["N_GROUPS"], seed=s)
    _, upd_pr, _ = srv_pr.run_round(b_pr.client_data, round_num=0,
                                    epochs=CONFIG["EPOCHS"])
    claimed = mean_output_prior_torch(CONFIG["ARCH"], upd_pr[CONFIG["ATTACKER"]].vec,
                                      b_pr.input_shape, b_pr.num_classes, b_pr.X_probe)

    for c in range(b_pr.num_classes):
        if own_pr[c] == 0:
            prior_rows.append({"seed": s, "class": c,
                               "attacker_holds": float(own_pr[c]),
                               "resampling_achieves": 0.0,
                               "target_wants": float(profile_pr[c]),
                               "prior_edit_claims": float(claimed[c])})

prior_edit = pd.DataFrame(prior_rows)
if len(prior_edit):
    show(prior_edit.round(4), "Classes the attacker holds NONE of")
    print()
    print("baseline: resampling leaves these at exactly 0.000, because a class you do")
    print("not hold cannot be drawn. That column is the norm this is measured against.")
    print()
    print(f"prior-editing claims {prior_edit['prior_edit_claims'].mean():.3f} on average,")
    print(f"against a target of {prior_edit['target_wants'].mean():.3f} and holdings of 0.")
    print()
    print("So the two routes differ in KIND. Resampling is bounded by what the attacker")
    print("owns; prior-editing is bounded by nothing, and yields a model that reports a")
    print("distribution it never learned.")
else:
    print("No zero-holding classes at this overlap, so the bound cannot be shown.")
    print("Lower CONFIG['OVERLAP'] to make the groups more disjoint.")
```

```
    1      8             0.0                  0.0        0.1246             0.1312
    2      9             0.0                  0.0        0.1553             0.1847

not hold cannot be drawn. That column is the norm this is measured against.

prior-editing claims 0.155 on average,
against a target of 0.146 and holdings of 0.

```

### The key line

```python
claimed = mean_output_prior_torch(CONFIG["ARCH"], upd_pr[CONFIG["ATTACKER"]].vec,
                                  b_pr.input_shape, b_pr.num_classes, b_pr.X_probe)
```

This takes the weight vector the attacker **actually submitted**, loads it into a fresh model,
runs it over the neutral probe set, and averages the softmax outputs. **It measures behaviour,
not intent.** It is the same function a server-side defence would use, which is what makes the
result meaningful as evidence about detectability.

`.vec` is the submitted flat parameter vector, what the server receives, after the attack
has done whatever it does.

### Why only one round

```python
_, upd_pr, _ = srv_pr.run_round(b_pr.client_data, round_num=0, ...)
```

The question is *what does the attacker's submission claim*, not *what happens to the
federation over time*. One round produces one submission, which is the whole object of study.
Running six rounds would cost six times as much and answer a question this cell is not asking.

### Reading the results *(Cell 21)*

Six rows, because the number of zero-holding classes varies by seed, one on seeds 0, 2, 3 and
4, and **two** on seed 1. The rows are per (seed, class), not per seed, which is why the table
has six rows from five seeds.

Every row: the attacker holds **0.0**, resampling achieves **0.0**, and prior-editing claims
something in the range **0.127 to 0.187**, against targets in the range 0.125 to 0.171. **One**
row slightly under-shoots (seed 3: 0.1266 against 0.1276); the other **five** over-shoot.

**Average: prior-editing claims 0.155 against a target of 0.146, from holdings of zero.**

### What this establishes, and what it does not

**Establishes:** the two routes differ in **kind**, not degree. Resampling yields a model that
has *learned* the distribution; prior-editing yields one that merely *reports* it. The
arithmetic in Cell 14 is confirmed by behaviour.

**Does not establish:** whether the claim survives contact with a server that checks. This is
stated explicitly as limitation 5 in the closing section. Prior-editing is measured for what it
**claims**: and that is exactly why it is the one *opening* for a defence that either study
leaves. A model whose reported prior and actual learned behaviour have come apart is in
principle detectable by a server willing to probe behaviour rather than read declarations,
which resampling is not. `DEFENSE_NOTES.md` §11.2 develops that, with three cautions attached.

### Why the `else` branch exists

```python
else:
    print("No zero-holding classes at this overlap, so the bound cannot be shown.")
    print("Lower CONFIG['OVERLAP'] to make the groups more disjoint.")
```

At a higher `OVERLAP` every client might hold at least one sample of every class, and the
comparison would be empty. Without this branch the cell would print an empty table and the
`.mean()` calls would produce NaN, a result that *looks* like a measurement and is not. **An
experiment that cannot run should say so, and say what to change.**

# Cells 22 to 23, Part 7: robust aggregation

## Cell 22, markdown

```markdown
## Part 7. Does robust aggregation change any of this?

Everything so far uses plain Federated Averaging, the weakest aggregator and one no serious
deployment would use alone. The standard robust rules are Krum, Multi-Krum, coordinate-wise
median, trimmed mean and Bulyan, reimplemented in `aggregation.py` from the published
equations and cross-checked against the ByzFL library.

The question splits in two, and the two halves have different answers:

- does the attacker still get **placed** in the target cluster?
- does the **damage** still land once it is inside?
```

**Why this part is necessary.** Everything before it uses plain FedAvg, and a reviewer's first
objection to any FL attack paper is "you attacked the weakest aggregator". This part answers
that objection with measurement.

**Why the question is split in two.** It is the finding. The two halves have different
answers, and a study that reported only one number would miss it entirely.

**Why reimplemented rather than imported.** Several of the authors' reference repositories
carry no licence. `aggregation.py` implements them from the published equations and
cross-checks against **ByzFL** (MIT-licensed) in a self-test.

**The six rules, briefly:**

| rule | how it works |
|---|---|
| **FedAvg** | plain mean of all updates. No robustness. |
| **Krum** | picks the *single* update closest to its nearest neighbours. Selection-based. |
| **Multi-Krum** | Krum repeated; averages the top `m` selected updates. |
| **coordinate-wise median** | per parameter, take the median across clients. Uses everyone. |
| **trimmed mean** | per parameter, drop the extremes and average the rest. Uses everyone. |
| **Bulyan** | Multi-Krum to select, then trimmed mean over the selection. Both mechanisms. |

The important split is **selection-based** (Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, reject the update
outright) versus **coordinate-wise** (median, trimmed mean, accept it but neutralise its
extreme coordinates during combination). Both contain the damage, by different means.

---

## Cell 23, code, the aggregator sweep

```python
# Placement and damage under each aggregation rule. The attacker resamples to the
# target and then amplifies, so both halves of the attack are present and can be
# scored separately.
#
# Fewer seeds here than elsewhere: six rules times two conditions is the most
# expensive cell in the notebook.
AGG_SEEDS = CONFIG["SEEDS"][:3]
AGGREGATORS = ("fedavg", "krum", "multikrum", "median", "trimmed", "bulyan")

agg_rows = []
for s in AGG_SEEDS:
    b_a = bundle(s)
    home_a, tgt_a, tgt_mem_a = sides(b_a)
    profile_a = group_profile(b_a, tgt_a)

    set_global_seeds(s, backend="torch")
    probe_a = SattlerCosineClusterer(eps1=-1.0, scope="head")
    warm_a = TorchFederatedServer(b_a.input_shape, b_a.num_classes, probe_a,
                                  arch=CONFIG["ARCH"],
                                  n_clusters=CONFIG["N_GROUPS"], seed=s)
    for r in range(4):
        _, wu, _ = warm_a.run_round(b_a.client_data, round_num=r,
                                    epochs=CONFIG["EPOCHS"])
    Dwa = stack([u.metadata["delta_vec"] for u in wu])[:, probe_a.head_index]
    ea1, ea2 = SattlerCosineClusterer(scope="head").tune_thresholds(Dwa, margin=1.5)

    for agg in AGGREGATORS:
        for label, beta, payload in (("control", 0.0, "none"),
                                     ("resample + boost x2", 1.0, "boost")):
            atk = ClusterSteering(
                malicious_clients=[CONFIG["ATTACKER"]], target_members=tgt_mem_a,
                mechanism="data", beta=beta, num_classes=b_a.num_classes,
                arch=CONFIG["ARCH"], input_shape=b_a.input_shape, seed=s,
                payload=payload, payload_scale=2.0)
            atk.target_hist = profile_a
            clus = SattlerCosineClusterer(eps1=ea1, eps2=ea2, scope="head",
                                          recursive=False,
                                          max_clusters=CONFIG["N_GROUPS"])
            set_global_seeds(s, backend="torch")
            srv_a = TorchFederatedServer(b_a.input_shape, b_a.num_classes,
                                         clus.reset(), arch=CONFIG["ARCH"],
                                         attack=atk, aggregator=agg,
                                         n_clusters=CONFIG["N_GROUPS"], seed=s)
            h_a = srv_a.fit(b_a.client_data, b_a.X_test, b_a.y_test,
                            rounds=CONFIG["ROUNDS"], epochs=CONFIG["EPOCHS"],
                            client_groups=b_a.groups)
            got = infiltration_of(h_a, CONFIG["ATTACKER"], tgt_mem_a)
            accs = [np.mean(list(e["metrics"].values())) for e in h_a]
            agg_rows.append({"seed": s, "aggregator": agg, "condition": label,
                             "infiltration": float(np.mean(got)) if got else np.nan,
                             "final_accuracy": float(accs[-1]) if accs else np.nan})

aggregation = pd.DataFrame(agg_rows)
save_run("dist_aggregators", aggregation, source="cfl-distribution.ipynb",
         note="six aggregation rules, control beside attacked, per-rule baselines",
         dataset=CONFIG["DATASET"], overlap=CONFIG["OVERLAP"])
show(aggregation.pivot_table(index="aggregator", columns="condition",
                             values="infiltration").round(3),
     "Placement under each aggregation rule (control beside attacked)")
show(aggregation.pivot_table(index="aggregator", columns="condition",
                             values="final_accuracy").round(3),
     "Accuracy under each rule")

print()
print("baseline: each rule is read against ITS OWN control, not against FedAvg. The")
print("rules do not all reach the same accuracy with no attacker present, so a shared")
print("reference would credit or penalise them for a difference the attack did not cause.")

analysis.plot_aggregator_outcome(aggregation, "docs/figures/dist_aggregators.png",
                                 attacked_label="resample + boost x2",
                                 acc_col="final_accuracy",
                                 title="Robust aggregation under distribution shift")

ctrl_a = aggregation[aggregation.condition == "control"].set_index(["seed", "aggregator"])
atk_a = aggregation[aggregation.condition != "control"].set_index(["seed", "aggregator"])
lost = (ctrl_a["final_accuracy"] - atk_a["final_accuracy"]).groupby("aggregator").mean()
print()
print("accuracy lost to the payload, against each rule's own control:")
for agg, v in lost.sort_values(ascending=False).items():
    print(f"  {agg:>10}: {v:+.4f}")

inf_atk = atk_a["infiltration"].mean()
inf_ctrl = ctrl_a["infiltration"].mean()
spread = atk_a.groupby("aggregator")["infiltration"].mean()
print()
print(f"placement: {inf_atk:.3f} attacked against {inf_ctrl:.3f} control, pooled")
print(f"across rules, range {spread.min():.3f} to {spread.max():.3f}")
print()
if spread.max() - spread.min() < 0.2:
    print("Placement is flat across every rule, so robust aggregation is not governing")
    print("it. Clustering decides who you are grouped with; aggregation decides whose")
    print("update counts. A robust aggregator only touches the second.")
else:
    print("Placement varies by rule, so the aggregator IS affecting who gets grouped")
    print("where, and the two decisions are not as separable as the concept-shift")
    print("notebook found them to be.")
```

### The payload

```python
payload="boost", payload_scale=2.0
```

After the attacker has resampled and trained, its delta is multiplied by 2. **Cosine
similarity is scale-invariant**, so doubling the delta does not change its *direction* at all,
the clusterer sees exactly the same update it would have seen anyway. The attacker keeps its
placement and doubles its influence on the average.

That is why placement and damage can be scored separately from the same run: the two halves of
the attack operate on different quantities. Placement is decided by direction; damage by
magnitude.

### Why three seeds instead of five

`AGG_SEEDS = CONFIG["SEEDS"][:3]`. Six rules × two conditions × six rounds × 12 clients is the
most expensive cell in the notebook, and the comment says so. **It is stated in the code, in
the output, and in the closing section's limitations** rather than left for a reader to notice
from a row count.

### Why each rule is read against its own control

This is the methodological point of the cell, and it is not cosmetic.

Look at the control column: krum reaches **0.756** with no attacker present, median **0.853**.
That is a spread of 0.10 that has nothing to do with the attack, Krum selects a single update
per round and discards eleven, so it simply learns more slowly.

If every rule were compared against FedAvg's control of 0.840, Krum would appear to "lose"
0.06 accuracy to an attack that did nothing to it, and median would appear to *gain*. **A
shared reference would credit or penalise each rule for a difference the attack did not
cause.**

### Reading the results *(Cell 23)*

**Placement: 1.000 under all six rules, control 0.000, range 1.000 to 1.000.** Perfectly flat.

**Damage: FedAvg loses 0.4119. Everything else loses nothing.** Multi-Krum's +0.0098 is
noise; the four negative values mean those rules ended marginally *higher* under attack than
in their own control, which is also noise. Only one number in that list is a real effect and
it is an order of magnitude larger than the rest.

### The finding

> **Clustering decides who you are grouped with; aggregation decides whose update counts. A
> robust aggregator governs only the second.**

Robust aggregation **contains the damage without preventing the intrusion**. An attacker whose
goal is *access* to a cluster's specialised model, rather than its destruction, pays no
price under any of the six rules.

**And this replicates the concept-shift study exactly**, with a different partitioner, a
different attack and different heterogeneity. One experiment showing this would be a finding;
two independent settings showing it is a **replication**, and that is what justifies
correcting the claim in the project report that spoofing defeats Byzantine-robust defences. It
does not: it defeats robust **clustering** completely and robust **aggregation** not at all.

### The `if/else` at the end

Again the cell derives its own conclusion. Had placement varied by more than 0.2 across rules,
it would have printed the opposite conclusion, that the aggregator *is* affecting who gets
grouped where, and that the two decisions are less separable than the other notebook found.
The notebook is written so it would report a disagreement between the two studies if one
existed.

# Cells 24 to 30, Parts 8, 9 and 10: the parameter campaign

> **These parts LOAD rather than COMPUTE.** Parts 1 to 7 run their own experiments inline.
> Parts 8 to 10 read results produced by `sweeps.py` and saved under `experiments/`. That
> split is deliberate: the campaign is about two hours of GPU time, and burying it in the
> notebook would make every re-execution cost two hours. It also follows the pattern
> `cfl-spoofing.ipynb` Part 7 already uses.

## Cell 24, markdown, the confound

```markdown
## Part 8. Is it imitation, or elimination? The group-count sweep

Everything above runs at **two** groups, and at two groups the headline number is ambiguous
in a way I did not account for at first.

> With two clusters, an attacker that merely stops resembling its **home** group has exactly
> one other place to go. It would land in the target **by elimination**, having imitated
> nothing at all, and that produces 1.000 infiltration just as a successful spoof does.

Two things settle it. Sweeping the number of groups, so that being evicted from home no
longer tells you where you land; and measuring **resemblance** directly, which is the
mechanism check this notebook did not previously have.

The decision rule was fixed before the run: high infiltration with positive resemblance is a
spoof; infiltration decaying toward the per-K control with negative resemblance is an
elimination artefact.
```

**What.** States a doubt about the notebook's own headline result, before testing it.

**Why this part exists at all.** Every infiltration number in Parts 5 to 7 is 1.000 at K=2,
and at K=2 that number cannot distinguish two very different stories. This is the same class
of error `RESULTS.md`'s method-notes table already records: *"infiltration 1.000 under
corruption / measurement taken after the split / caught by the resemblance column"*. The
concept-shift study caught it via `part_b/ladder.py`; this study had never checked.

**Why the decision rule is written down first.** It is the whole point. Stating in advance
what result would *falsify* the headline is what stops the outcome being read to fit the
conclusion already in the write-up. Had infiltration decayed toward the per-K control with
resemblance going negative, `RESULTS.md` Part A would have needed rewriting rather than
extending.

---

## Cell 25, code, the group-count sweep, loaded and guarded

```python
# Loaded, not recomputed: `python sweeps.py groups` produced this. The guard
# refuses the file if its configuration is not what this cell claims -- it
# checks the CONFIGURATION, not just the condition names, so a file produced at
# a different number of rounds cannot be presented here as if it were this one.
from run_context import load_experiment

groups = load_experiment("02_n_groups_2-3-4-6",
                         expect=dict(dataset="mnist", rounds=6, n_attackers=1))

atk_g = groups[~groups.is_control.astype(bool)]
ctl_g = groups[groups.is_control.astype(bool)]
tab = (atk_g.groupby("n_groups")
       .agg(infiltration=("infiltration", "mean"),
            resemblance=("target_resemblance", "mean"))
       .join(ctl_g.groupby("n_groups")
             .agg(control=("infiltration", "mean"),
                  control_resemblance=("target_resemblance", "mean")))
       .reset_index())
tab["1/K (chance)"] = (1.0 / tab["n_groups"]).round(3)
show(tab.round(3), "Placement and mechanism against the number of planted groups")

analysis.plot_confound_panel(groups,
                             "experiments/02_n_groups_2-3-4-6/graphs/confound_panel.png")

print()
print("baseline: each K against ITS OWN measured control. At K=3 and K=6 the")

res_lo = atk_g.groupby("n_groups")["target_resemblance"].mean().min()
if flat.min() > 0.9 and res_lo > 0:
```

### The guard is the important line

```python
groups = load_experiment("02_n_groups_2-3-4-6",
                         expect=dict(dataset="mnist", rounds=6, n_attackers=1))
```

This refuses the file unless every pinned value matches in **every row**, no pinned column
*varies*, and every experimental cell has a control row.

**Why that is stronger than the guards it replaces.** `cfl-spoofing.ipynb` cells 25 and 27
check the condition set and the seed count, which catches a wrong *treatment*: but the old
result files never recorded how many rounds or groups produced them, so a file generated at
`rounds=8` would be silently accepted and displayed as `rounds=6`. Every campaign row now
carries its full 47-column configuration, which is what makes a configuration check possible
at all. `HANDOFF.md` records **four** incidents of stale results being pooled with fresh ones;
this is the machinery that makes a fifth loud instead of silent.

### Reading the result *(Cell 25)*

**Infiltration is flat at 1.000 while destinations multiply.** At K=6 there are five wrong
clusters and one right one. Elimination predicts roughly 1/(K−1), and the measured value does
not move at all.

**Resemblance is positive and rises**: +0.725 to +1.219, against controls hugging zero.
Elimination predicts the opposite: a client pushed away from its home group without imitating
anyone shows flat or negative resemblance.

**The controls are not zero at K=3 and K=6.** 0.333 and 0.222 respectively. The server
misplaces *honest* clients at those settings, so the attack's real gap is 0.667 and 0.778
rather than 1.000. Reading them against zero would credit the attack with the environment's
own failures, which is why the column is printed beside every number.

**One check made outside the notebook.** `recursive=False` splits at most once per round,
raising the possibility that "K=6" was really a two-cluster experiment. It is not: splits
persist, so the tree accumulates 2 → 4 → **6** clusters by round 2 and holds. Verified
directly; the K=6 result is a genuine six-destination test.

**A conclusion computed, not typed.** The `if/else` means a future run that decayed would
print the opposite verdict. The notebook cannot silently drift out of agreement with its own
data.

## Cell 26, markdown, Part 9 framing

```markdown
## Part 9. Attacker count, and how long the federation runs

Two of the limitations this notebook concedes, measured rather than conceded.

**Attacker fraction.** One attacker in twelve is 8.3%, where the literature runs 1 to 30%.

**Federation length.** Six rounds is short. Splits in this implementation are *permanent* --
the cluster tree is only refined, never re-merged -- so placement should lock early and hold.
If infiltration fell as rounds rose, that assumption would be wrong.
```

**Why these two together.** Both are limitations the closing section previously *conceded*
rather than measured, and both are cheap to sweep. The rounds prediction is again stated
before the run, with the falsifying outcome named.

---

## Cell 27, code, attacker count and federation length

```python
# Both sweeps, side by side. Each row is read against its own control at the
# same setting, never against a shared reference.
for name, factor, label in (("03_attackers_1-2-3", "n_attackers", "malicious clients of 12"),
                            ("04_rounds_6-12-20-30", "rounds", "federated rounds")):
    d = load_experiment(name)
    a = d[~d.is_control.astype(bool)]
    c = d[d.is_control.astype(bool)]
    t = (a.groupby(factor).agg(infiltration=("infiltration", "mean"),
                               resemblance=("target_resemblance", "mean"),
                               accuracy=("final_accuracy", "mean"))
         .join(c.groupby(factor).agg(control=("infiltration", "mean"),
                                     control_accuracy=("final_accuracy", "mean")))
         .reset_index())
    show(t.round(3), f"Sweeping {label}")

print()
print("Placement is 1.000 at 25% malicious and still 1.000 after 30 rounds, against")
print("a 0.000 control throughout. The attack does not need numbers -- one client")
print("that genuinely resembles the target is already sufficient -- and a defence")
print("cannot wait it out, because the cluster tree never re-merges.")
print()
print("Resemblance is identical across the rounds sweep by construction: it is")
print("measured PRE-SPLIT during a fixed 4-round warmup, which does not change")
print("when the number of rounds does. Measuring it after a split would compare")
print("deltas taken from different starting points, which is not like-for-like.")
```

**Attacker fraction closes the limitation without producing a new finding**, which is worth
saying plainly. 8.3% was never doing any work: a single client that genuinely resembles the
target is already sufficient, so adding more changes nothing. That is a *stronger* statement
than "it also works with more attackers".

> **A bug this sweep exposed.** Attackers were originally chosen as clients 0…n−1 *by index*.
> Group assignment is shuffled per seed, and on all three seeds one of clients {0,1,2} was
> already a member of the **target** group, a client with nothing to infiltrate. The control
> caught it, reading 0.5 and 0.333 instead of 0.000, and `sweeps.run_cell` now selects
> attackers from the attacker's own home group. The first run's data was discarded rather than
> reinterpreted. This is the second time in this project that **a control behaving oddly
> revealed a measurement error rather than a result**.

**Rounds confirms the permanence prediction.** Five times the training changes nothing. Both
conditions climb in accuracy and the attacker's federation stays marginally ahead throughout.

**Why resemblance is identical at every round count**, which looks like a bug and is not: it
is measured **pre-split**, during a fixed 4-round warmup that does not change when `rounds`
does. Only the training *after* placement varies. Measuring it post-split would compare deltas
referenced against different starting models, not like-for-like, and a mistake this project
made once already.

**The defence consequence is concrete.** There is no round count at which the server recovers,
because the tree never re-merges. Detection must happen in the 3-to-5 round window before the
split, or not at all.

### Two predictions that were wrong, and why that is the useful part

**Epochs.** The prediction was that more local training sharpens the server's clustering
signal and makes the attack harder. Placement never moves, but **resemblance decays
monotonically**, +0.758 → +0.665. So the effect is real and in the predicted direction; the
attack simply has enough margin to absorb it.

This is exactly why the campaign reports **outcome and mechanism side by side**. A figure
plotting infiltration alone would show four identical points and conclude "epochs do not
matter". The mechanism column shows they do, just not enough, a different and more useful
statement, and the one that would let someone predict where the attack *would* break.

**Data.** The prediction was that more data helps the server. It helps the **attacker**
(+0.785 → +0.908). The reasoning behind the prediction considered only one side: the attacker
resamples from its own data too, so its imitation sharpens along with everyone else's updates.
The attack does not exploit noise, so removing noise does not remove it. **At the full
60,000-sample MNIST set, 5,000 per client, infiltration is still 1.000**, which answers the
"small-data artefact" objection directly.

### The two frontiers, and why only the controls tell them apart

| | attack | control | separation (Part 1 metric) | what failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| concentration 5 | 0.000 | **0.333** | 2.14 | the **environment** |
| overlap 0.0 | 0.000 | **0.000** | **17.31** | the **attack** |

Both read 0.000, and they mean opposite things.

At **concentration 5** the clusterer misplaces honest clients a third of the time, and
separation is 2.14, barely above the Dirichlet ceiling of 1.65 measured in Part 1. There is
no coherent group to join, so this is not a statement about the attack at all.

At **overlap 0.0** the environment is at its strongest anywhere in the campaign and the
control is perfect, yet the attack achieves nothing and resemblance collapses to the control
band. The cause is the bound derived in Part 3: disjoint groups mean the attacker holds
**none** of the target's classes, so resampling manufactures nothing. **Part 3 showed that on
one class arithmetically; this shows it where it binds on every class at once, and the
prediction is exact.**

> The configuration that defeats the attack is fully disjoint groups, which is also the
> configuration where Clustered Federated Learning has least reason to exist, since disjoint
> groups can simply be trained as separate models. That tension belongs in the report rather
> than presenting zero overlap as a mitigation.

**Resemblance tracks overlap almost linearly** (+0.084 → +0.491 → +0.725 → +1.299), which
states the mechanism directly: the attack's strength is the size of the intersection between
what the attacker holds and what the target looks like.

### The limitation the cell prints about itself

`campaign_summary` is **generated** by `analysis.campaign_summary`, using the same
`compare_to_baseline` machinery as everywhere else, so the verdicts cannot drift from the
data. It reports concentration 10 and overlap 0.15 as *not distinguishable* despite gaps of
0.667, correct, and the machinery being conservative: with three seeds, a 2-of-3 outcome
cannot be separated from a 0-of-3 control.

**The endpoints are solid; the transitions are not.** Where each frontier lies exactly is
unresolved by this run, and quoting 0.667 as a point estimate would overstate what three seeds
support.

# Cells 31 to 32, Part 11: which target does the attacker pick?

Added 27 Aug 2026, after `experiments/10_target_choice/` had been run. Appended here
rather than inserted earlier on purpose: putting it before Cell 30 would renumber cells that
are cited by name in this file, `PRESENTATION.md` and `SLIDES.md`.

## Cell 31, markdown, the question and the prediction

## Part 11. Does it matter WHICH group the attacker picks?

Everything above fixed the victim: `sides()` took the first other group in sorted order
and nothing ever varied it. At K>2 that is a free choice the attacker actually has, and it
had never been exercised.

**The prediction, fixed before the run: the most DIFFUSE target should be easiest.** A
diffuse group's mean histogram sits near uniform, and uniform is what a `blind` attacker
declares, so its estimate should be most accurate there. The Part 3 resampling bound should
also bite less, since a spread-out profile is more likely built from classes the attacker
already holds.

Scored on **resemblance**, not infiltration, decided in advance: infiltration was saturated
at 1.000 across every other factor in the campaign, and a saturated metric cannot show a
difference between targets.

## Cell 32, code, the target sweep, loaded and tested within seeds

```python
# Loaded, not recomputed: `python sweeps.py targets` produced this, 80 rows.
# Two predictors per row, and the confound must be reported beside the hypothesis:
#   target_spread   JS from the target's mean profile to uniform. LOW means diffuse,
#                   which is the condition the prediction says is EASIER.
#   home_to_target  JS from the attacker's home profile to the target's. The rival
#                   explanation: a target that resembles your own group is easier for
#                   reasons that have nothing to do with how diffuse it is.
from scipy import stats

tgt = load_experiment("10_target_choice")
atk = tgt[~tgt.is_control.astype(bool)]

# WITHIN-SEED, not pooled. `target_rank` is not a stable identity across seeds: the
# attacker's home is wherever client 0 landed and group assignment is shuffled, so
# "rank 1" is a different real group each time. Pooling mixes between-seed variation
# in and hides the effect.
rho = [stats.spearmanr(g.target_spread, g.target_resemblance)[0]
       for _, g in atk.groupby(["n_groups", "seed"])]
pos = sum(r > 0 for r in rho)
p = stats.binomtest(pos, len(rho), 0.5).pvalue

med = atk.target_spread.median()
halves = pd.DataFrame({
    "mean target_spread": [atk[atk.target_spread < med].target_spread.mean(),
                           atk[atk.target_spread >= med].target_spread.mean()],
    "mean resemblance":   [atk[atk.target_spread < med].target_resemblance.mean(),
                           atk[atk.target_spread >= med].target_resemblance.mean()],
}, index=["diffuse targets", "peaked targets"]).round(4)
show(halves, "Resemblance by how diffuse the target is")

# boot_ci returns (mean, lo, hi), three values, as every other cell in this
# notebook unpacks it. Use it rather than an ad-hoc bootstrap so the intervals
# quoted in the write-up come from the project's ONE standard estimator.
for lab, s in (("diffuse", atk[atk.target_spread < med]),
               ("peaked ", atk[atk.target_spread >= med])):
    m, lo, hi = boot_ci(s.target_resemblance.values)
    print(f"  {lab} half  resemblance {m:.4f} [{lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f}]")

rh, ph = stats.spearmanr(atk.home_to_target, atk.target_resemblance)
print(f"\n{pos} of {len(rho)} (K, seed) blocks slope POSITIVE, sign test p={p:.4f}")
print(f"the confound explains nothing: resemblance vs home_to_target "
      f"rho={rh:+.3f}, p={ph:.3f}")

if pos == len(rho):
    print("\nThe prediction is FALSIFIED, and consistently. Peaked targets are easier to")
    print("resemble than diffuse ones, which is the opposite of what we wrote down.")
    print("Resemblance is a RELATIVE measure: imitating a diffuse target makes the")
    print("attacker look like everybody, which marks it as a member of nobody. A peaked")
    print("target is distinctive, so imitating it lands somewhere specific.")
else:
    print(f"\n{pos}/{len(rho)} blocks positive: not the clean reversal the write-up claims.")
    print("Re-check before quoting section 3.9.")
```

```

Resemblance by how diffuse the target is
                 mean target_spread  mean resemblance
diffuse targets               0.168            0.9941
peaked targets                0.238            1.1784
  diffuse half  resemblance 0.9941 [0.8559, 1.1177]
  peaked  half  resemblance 1.1784 [1.1300, 1.2303]

10 of 10 (K, seed) blocks slope POSITIVE, sign test p=0.0020
the confound explains nothing: resemblance vs home_to_target rho=+0.037, p=0.821

The prediction is FALSIFIED, and consistently. Peaked targets are easier to
resemble than diffuse ones, which is the opposite of what we wrote down.
Resemblance is a RELATIVE measure: imitating a diffuse target makes the
attacker look like everybody, which marks it as a member of nobody. A peaked
target is distinctive, so imitating it lands somewhere specific.
```

**What.** Loads the 80 rows `python sweeps.py targets` produced, splits them at the median
`target_spread`, and tests whether the attacker does better against diffuse targets.

**Why the test is within-seed and not pooled.** `target_rank` is not a stable identity across
seeds. The attacker's home is wherever client 0 landed and group assignment is shuffled, so
"rank 1" is a different real group on every seed. Pooling all 40 attacked rows mixes
between-seed variation into the estimate and hides the effect: pooled, the correlation reads
+0.260 with an interval crossing zero, which looks like nothing happened. **Do not quote the
pooled figure.**

**Why `boot_ci` and not something hand-rolled.** The first version of this cell used an ad-hoc
bootstrap written in a scratch script, which gave [0.8490, 1.1243] and [1.1290, 1.2313].
Close, but not the project's own estimator, and two bootstraps in one repository is exactly
how two documents end up quoting different intervals for the same quantity. Every interval in
this notebook now comes from `run_context.boot_ci`.

**Why the cell decides its own conclusion.** The `if/else` prints the falsification only when
all ten blocks agree. If a re-run produced nine, the cell would print a warning naming
section 3.9 instead, rather than a conclusion the data no longer supports. That is
Appendix B rule 4.

**The result.** The prediction was **falsified**: peaked targets are easier to resemble than
diffuse ones, 10 of 10 blocks, sign test p = 0.0020, with the confound clean at rho +0.037,
p = 0.821. Section 3.9 of the lecture explains why it reverses.

# Cell 33, the closing section

```markdown
## What this establishes

Parts 1 to 7 are measured at one configuration; Parts 8 to 10 sweep it. Every number is
against its own measured control.

**The setting is not a free choice.** Statistical heterogeneity only supports a clustering
study when the heterogeneity is *grouped*. Dirichlet partitioning, the standard
non-Independent-and-Identically-Distributed generator, gives every client its own skew and
no group structure: across concentration 0.05 to 1.0, the best two-way split that exists
*anywhere* in it scores 1.43 to 1.65, against a median random split of 0.99. Planted
profiles score 4.51 at the operating point and 17.31 when disjoint. A study run on Dirichlet
is measuring infiltration into an arbitrary set of clients.

**Both channels give the server something real, and both are spoofable.**

| channel | server recovers groups at | attacked | control |
|---|---|---|---|
| declared label histogram | ARI **1.000** | **1.000** | 0.000 |
| inferred from updates | AUC **1.000** on the head | **1.000** | 0.000 |

**Imitation is free.** Resampling to the target reaches 1.000 infiltration while accuracy
moves 0.833 to 0.843, which is *not distinguishable* from the no-attack control. Resampling
changes which distribution the model learns, not how well it learns one, so the attacker
pays no visible price for the disguise and a defence looking for a degraded attacker will
not find one.

**The two imitation routes differ in kind, not degree.** On classes the attacker holds
**none** of, resampling achieves exactly 0.000, because a class you do not hold cannot be
drawn. Prior-editing claims **0.155** on those same classes against a target of 0.146.
Resampling yields a model that has *learned* the distribution; prior-editing yields one that
merely *reports* it.

**The binding constraint is knowledge, not capability.** Estimating the target's
distribution by probing the broadcast model gives error 0.0844 against 0.0887 for assuming
uniform and never probing at all. The intervals overlap, so the two are **not
distinguishable**. An attacker *told* the distribution imitates it perfectly and for free;
an attacker that must *work it out* from what the server broadcasts cannot.

**Robust aggregation does not prevent the intrusion.** Placement is **1.000 under all six
rules** against a 0.000 control, range 1.000 to 1.000. Damage lands only under plain
Federated Averaging, which loses 0.41 accuracy against its own control while every robust
rule loses nothing. Clustering decides who you are grouped with, aggregation decides whose
update counts, and a robust aggregator governs only the second.

> This replicates the concept-shift result in `cfl-spoofing.ipynb` exactly. The same
> structural finding under two different kinds of heterogeneity is a replication rather than
> a single experiment, and it is the evidence for correcting the claim in the project report
> that spoofing defeats Byzantine-robust defences. It does not: it defeats robust
> *clustering* completely and robust *aggregation* not at all.

**It is imitation, not elimination.** At two groups, an attacker evicted from its home group
lands in the target by default, which looks identical to a spoof. Sweeping to 6 groups leaves
five wrong destinations and one right one, and infiltration does not move from **1.000** while
resemblance *rises* to **+1.219**. Elimination would predict roughly 1/(K-1) and a flat or
negative resemblance. This is the mechanism check the notebook previously lacked.

**Placement is invariant across four factors**: up to **25%** of clients malicious, **30**
rounds, **10** local epochs, and the full **60,000**-sample MNIST training set. It is not a
small-data or short-run artefact.

**Two frontiers exist, and they fail for opposite reasons.** Below concentration 10 the attack
fails, but so does the clusterer on honest clients (control 0.333), so that is the environment
collapsing rather than a defence. At **zero overlap** the attack fails while the environment is
at its strongest (separation 17.31, control 0.000), because disjoint groups leave the attacker
holding none of the target's classes and resampling with nothing to draw from. **That is the
Part 3 bound confirmed where it binds on every class at once.**

## What this does not establish

1. **One dataset, one architecture.** MNIST with a Multi-Layer Perceptron.
2. ~~One attacker in twelve.~~ **Closed by Part 9**: swept to 3 of 12 (25%), placement 1.000
   throughout.
3. **The aggregator sweep uses three seeds**, not five, being the most expensive cell here.
4. **No defence is measured**, by choice. There is therefore no false positive rate.
5. **Prior-editing is measured for what it CLAIMS**, through the model's output distribution,
   not for whether that claim survives contact with a server that checks behaviour.
6. **The sweeps use three seeds**, which resolves a frontier's endpoints but not its middle: a
   2-of-3 outcome cannot be separated from a 0-of-3 control, so intermediate points report
   *not distinguishable*. The two frontier locations are unresolved.
7. **The campaign is one factor at a time**, so interactions between parameters are not
   measured. Full factorial over five factors is hundreds of GPU-hours.
```

**Why this cell is the only one with static numbers.** Every other conclusion is computed by
the cell that produced it, so it cannot drift. This one is markdown quoting fixed values,
mitigated by the notebook being deterministic (three consecutive executions have reproduced it
identically) but it is the one place to re-check after a parameter change.

**Why "What this does not establish" is a section rather than a sentence.** An examiner will
find these. Volunteering them is more honest and more persuasive than being led to them, and
each is specific enough to act on. Item 2 is struck through rather than deleted, so the record
shows a limitation that was **measured away** rather than quietly dropped.

**A note on what this cell used to say.** Before 24 August it read *"Open in this notebook. The
payload, robust aggregation, and the multi-seed grid are not here yet"*: false, since Parts 5,
6 and 7 covered all three. Before the campaign it still listed the attacker fraction as an open
limitation, after Part 9 had closed it. Both are arguments for auditing the prose around
results as carefully as the results themselves.

# Appendix A: vocabulary

| term | meaning |
|---|---|
| **ARI** (Adjusted Rand Index) | Agreement between two partitions, chance-corrected. Random = 0.0, perfect = 1.0. For 12 clients in 2 groups of 6: **0.665 is exactly one client misplaced**, 0.396 is two. |
| **AUC** (Area Under the Curve) | Probability a random within-group pair is more similar than a random cross-group pair. 0.5 chance, 1.0 perfect separation. |
| **margin** | mean within-group similarity minus mean cross-group similarity. Reported beside AUC because the two disagree usefully: the full vector scores AUC 0.885 with margin 0.0002. |
| **resemblance** | The attacker's cosine similarity to the target group, read against the honest bands. Near 0 means "looks like a stranger", large positive means "looks like a member". **The mechanism check**: infiltration says the server *placed* the attacker, resemblance says whether it *looked like* a member. |
| **Jensen-Shannon divergence** | Symmetric, bounded distance between two distributions. 0 when identical. Used instead of cosine because cosine scores a spread vector against a peaked one highly regardless of whether they describe the same distribution. |
| **separation ratio** | cross-group JS divided by within-group JS. **1.0 = no group structure.** Unstable where within-group divergence approaches zero, which is why the K=6 / overlap-0 cell scores 202 and is not quoted. |
| **total variation distance** | Half the summed absolute difference. How much probability mass must move to turn one distribution into the other. |
| **infiltration** | Fraction of *post-split* rounds in which the attacker shared a cluster with the majority of the target group. Baseline is the **measured honest control**, not 1/K. |
| **beta** | The attacker's commitment dial, 0 to 1. `beta=0` reduces every mechanism to honest behaviour and is the control. |
| **payload** | What the attacker does *after* getting in. `boost` multiplies its delta by `payload_scale`; cosine is scale-invariant so this does not affect placement. |
| **delta** | Submitted weights minus received weights. What the client actually contributes this round. |
| **head / head scope** | The final Linear layer's weight and bias. `scope="head"` restricts similarity to these, following FedRep and FedPer. |
| **probe set** | Held-out data the server owns, disjoint from every client's data and from the test set. Used to measure model *behaviour* rather than read declarations. |
| **bootstrap CI** | Confidence interval by resampling the observed values. Overlapping intervals mean *not distinguishable*. |
| **oracle / inferred / blind** | The three attacker-knowledge levels. `blind` is the baseline the others must beat. |
| **concentration** | How tightly each client's histogram hugs its group's profile. High means within-group clients are nearly identical. Sets how hard the clustering problem is. |
| **overlap** | Fraction of each group's label mass spread uniformly over *all* classes rather than its own block. `overlap=0` gives disjoint class supports. |
| **FedAvg** | Plain averaging of client updates. The non-robust default. |
| **Krum / Multi-Krum / Bulyan** | Selection-based robust aggregators: they *reject* suspicious updates. |
| **median / trimmed mean** | Coordinate-wise robust aggregators: they *accept* every update but neutralise extreme values per parameter. |
| **BatchNorm buffers** | Running mean and variance. They track **input** statistics, are near-identical across clients, and dominate the update's magnitude, which is why full-vector clustering fails on this architecture. |
| **the schema** | The 47 columns every campaign row carries (`run_context.SWEEP_COLUMNS`): provenance, the **complete** configuration, the condition, the measurements. Not just the varied factor. |
| **the guard** | `run_context.load_experiment(name, expect=...)`. Refuses a file whose pinned configuration does not match, whose pinned column *varies*, or where a treatment cell has no control row. |

---

# Appendix B: the rules this notebook follows

Each is a response to something that went wrong at least once. They generalise beyond this
notebook.

**1. Every number gets a control, measured on the same setup.** Not a theoretical baseline,
not 1/K, but the same experiment with the attack switched off, same seeds, same code path.

**2. Where the gap is smaller than the intervals, say *not distinguishable*.** The accuracy
row in Cell 19 is the example: 0.843 against 0.833 is reported as no effect, not a small one.

**3. Show per-seed values for every headline number.** A mean over five seeds can hide a
single seed carrying the result. Cell 16's per-seed table shows `inferred` losing to `blind`
on seed 2, which is the honest picture.

**4. Let the cell compute its own conclusion.** The `if/else` blocks in Cells 16, 19, 23 and
25 mean the prose cannot drift out of agreement with the numbers above it. Only the final
markdown cell contains static values.

**5. Tune on attacker-free data.** Any threshold fitted in the presence of the attack
describes a server that has already seen what we claim it cannot see.

**6. Print what a tuning step chose.** The `[sattler]` lines exist because threshold tuning
failed **silently, twice, in opposite directions**: once shattering the federation into
singletons, once making the split criterion permanently unsatisfiable. Neither raised an error.

**7. Make an unrunnable experiment say so.** Cell 21's `else` branch prints why the comparison
is empty and what to change, instead of emitting an empty table and NaN means that look like
measurements.

**8. Assert the preconditions a shortcut might break.** `QUICK` mode once silently removed a
study's control condition. The assert in Cell 4 makes that impossible.

**9. Measure behaviour, not intent, when the claim is about behaviour.** Cell 14 derives the
bias shift; Cell 21 loads the submitted weights and reads the model's actual output. The
second is what makes "unbounded" evidence rather than algebra.

**10. Score the geometry before the algorithm acts on it.** `eps1=-1.0` holds the federation
open so update geometry is measured against one consistent reference, separately from any
clustering decision made using it.

**11. Track membership by who, never by cluster name.** Cluster identifiers are reassigned
every round.

**12. Every row carries its complete configuration**, not just the varied factor. It makes a
row self-describing, lets any two experiments concatenate, and lets a guard check the
*configuration* rather than only the condition names. `HANDOFF.md` records four incidents of
stale results pooled with fresh ones; this is what makes a fifth detectable.

**13. State the falsifying outcome before the run.** Part 8's decision rule was fixed in
advance, naming what result would have meant the headline was an artefact. It is what stops a
result being read to fit the conclusion already in the write-up.

**14. Report a measurement you cannot make as absent, not as a number.** The FEMNIST payload
in the other notebook sits at the control level, so it is reported as unmeasured rather than
as a result. Likewise the frontier midpoints here, which three seeds cannot resolve.

**15. Anything run unattended must be resumable.** On this machine a process death is an
out-of-memory kill and it is silent. The extremes sweep did crash partway; resume meant it
cost one cell rather than the whole run.

**16. A summary statistic that confirms the hypothesis is the one to distrust.** Six results
in this project began as a confident number that agreed with expectation while the mechanism
underneath had changed. **Every one was caught by a breakdown, by round, by parameter scope,
by seed, and none by the headline figure.** `F_ATTEMPTS.md` has the full account.
